zh.summary: 從醫院報到、六行業情境與收件系統，理解 HCI、UI、UX、易用性及可驗證的 AI 設計需求。
objectives: 以工作情境區分 HCI、UI 與 UX 的分析範圍。
指出美觀、易用與整體任務結果之間的差異。
為一個介面困難提出可觀察的修改假設。

readingGuide.goal: 以工作情境區分 HCI、UI 與 UX 的分析範圍。
readingGuide.startingPoint: problem.md、文字編輯器與合成收件情境；不需要改程式或接觸真人。
readingGuide.route: 先看情境與原理，再比較例子，最後擴寫 wireframe-notes.md 並用檢核題自查。
readingGuide.output: 一份包含三種分析觀點、具體修改假設及待驗方法的 wireframe-notes.md。

sections.heading: 讓使用者理解系統並完成工作
paragraphs: 這堂課最重要的一句話：設計系統的目的，不是讓使用者欣賞介面，而是讓使用者能夠理解系統、正確操作，最後順利完成自己真正想做的事情。
本課從日常生活、醫療、銀行、物流、政府服務及 AI 軟體開發等情境學習。

sections.heading: 一、先用一個生活例子理解三者
paragraphs: 想像今天你到醫院看診，必須使用醫院的自助報到機。
你走到機器前，插入健保卡，確認掛號資料，完成報到，再前往診間候診。
這件看似簡單的事情，其實包含三種不同的設計問題。

blocks.caption: 圖 1｜醫院報到的三種設計問題
blocks.description: UI、HCI、UX 是並列的分析視角；使用者的目標是順利就醫。

items.title: UI — User Interface（使用者介面）
items.body:
報到機螢幕上的按鈕、字體、顏色、文字提示、插卡指示等，應該如何呈現？

例如：「確認報到」按鈕是否太小？長輩能不能看清楚？

items.title: HCI — Human–Computer Interaction（人機互動）
items.body:
人如何理解機器的指示、判斷下一步，以及操作機器？

例如：畫面寫著「完成」，病人以為已經看診報到，但系統其實只確認健保卡讀取成功。為什麼會誤解？

items.title: UX — User Experience（使用者經驗）
items.body:
從到醫院、報到、候診、看診、領藥到離院，整體經驗好不好？

例如：報到機操作只要 20 秒，但報到後沒有告訴病人診間在哪裡，病人還是可能迷路。

paragraphs: 這個例子最重要的地方在於：
報到機的 UI 可以很好看、操作也很簡單，但整體 UX 依然可能很糟糕。
原因是使用者真正要完成的工作，是順利就醫，而不是成功操作報到機。
這也是 Nielsen Norman Group 對 UX 的經典觀點：使用者經驗涉及使用者與產品、服務及組織互動的整體過程，不能只用介面好不好看來判斷。

sections.heading: 二、三個概念究竟有什麼差別？
paragraphs: 先比較各自關注的問題與方法，再判斷要蒐集什麼證據。

blocks.caption: 表 1｜HCI、UI、UX 比較
rows: 整段經驗是否符合需求？
完成任務，順利取得服務

paragraphs: 需要特別澄清：HCI、UI、UX 不是三個完全分開的工作階段，也不是誰一定包含誰。
HCI 是跨領域的研究與設計領域；UI 是人與系統互動的接觸介面；UX 是使用者經驗的整體品質。三者有很大的交集。

blocks.caption: 圖 2｜HCI、UI、UX 與互動設計的交會
blocks.description: 參考 Figma 的概念示意。交疊表示關注點互相影響，不是嚴格的學術集合分類，也不表示三個先後階段。

items.title: HCI｜人機互動
items.body: 人的認知、行為與互動能力

items.title: UI｜使用者介面
items.body: 畫面、控制元件與回應

items.title: UX｜使用者經驗
items.body: 整段服務的需求、結果與感受

items.title: IxD｜互動設計
items.body: 設計互動行為與回饋，涉及三種觀點的交會

paragraphs: Figma 的概念示意圖：HCI、UI 與 UX 彼此重疊，而 Interaction Design（互動設計）涉及三者的交會。這是理解關係的示意，不是嚴格的學術集合分類。
還有一個容易誤解的地方：UI 不一定是螢幕。語音助理的語音提示、車輛的實體控制面板、ATM 的操作按鍵，都可以是使用者介面。

sections.heading: 三、HCI：為什麼使用者會誤解系統？
paragraphs: HCI 是三者之中最值得深入理解的基礎之一，因為軟體工程師知道系統怎麼運作，不代表使用者也知道。
舉例來說，一個銀行系統顯示「審核完成」。
工程師的意思可能是：「系統已完成資料完整性檢查。」
但是銀行職員可能理解成：「這筆貸款已經通過審核。」
同樣四個字，雙方卻有完全不同的理解。
這涉及 HCI 的一個重要概念：Mental Model（心智模型）。

blocks.heading: 1. Mental Model：每個人心中都有自己的系統操作地圖
paragraphs: 你第一次使用陌生的洗衣機，可能會根據過去的經驗，猜測「開始」按鈕按下去後會立刻洗衣。
但這台洗衣機可能先要求你選擇水量、洗程和溫度。
這就是使用者心中的預期，與系統實際運作方式不一致。
良好的人機互動設計，應該盡量讓系統行為符合使用者的合理預期，或提供足夠資訊協助使用者形成正確理解。

blocks.heading: 2. Feedback：操作之後，系統必須回應
paragraphs: 假設你在購物網站按下「付款」。
結果畫面完全沒有反應。
你不知道付款是否成功，於是又按了一次，可能造成重複訂單。
這是典型的 Feedback（回饋）問題。
好的系統需要告訴你目前狀態，例如「正在處理付款」、「付款成功，訂單編號為……」或「付款失敗，尚未扣款」。

blocks.heading: 3. Error Prevention：避免使用者犯錯，而不只是事後顯示錯誤
paragraphs: 例如藥局系統允許藥師將藥品加入領藥清單。
如果某筆處方的藥品劑量異常，系統不應只在最後出現模糊的「錯誤代碼 203」。
更好的做法可能包括明確標示異常內容、協助核對原始處方，並依專業規範要求適當確認。
這些設計涉及人如何理解資訊、做出決策，以及如何減少操作失誤。
上述三種概念，都與 Nielsen 的可用性設計原則相符，包括系統狀態可見性、使用者熟悉的語言，以及錯誤預防。

sections.heading: 四、用六個不同行業的例子加深理解
paragraphs: 以下均為假設情境，用來練習從不同角度找問題。

blocks.caption: 表 2｜六行業的分析視角
rows: 病人誤認為選日期就已掛號
預約後到現場仍找不到報到位置
客戶分不清資料檢查與核貸通過
線上申請後還須臨櫃重填
包裹送達錯誤地點，申訴困難
學生不知道是否完成測驗
課程完成後仍不知道如何應用
操作員搞不清警報優先順序
排除異常後無法順利復工
使用者不知道 AI 是否正在聆聽
AI 正確辨識語音，卻無法完成預約

paragraphs: 注意，這張表不是在說每個問題只能歸入一種分類。
例如「配送中」的文字可能同時是 UI 的資訊呈現問題、HCI 的理解問題，以及 UX 的配送期待落差。
實際設計時，三者是互補的分析視角，不是互斥的問題類別。

sections.heading: 五、從使用者的行動流程看清楚三者關係
paragraphs: 我們可以把一個互動系統理解成以下過程。

blocks.caption: 圖 3｜從使用者目標到整體結果
blocks.description: 簡化的教學流程。實際操作通常會反覆經過「操作、回饋、理解、再操作」的循環；HCI 與 UX 也涵蓋比圖中更廣的範圍。 UI 與 HCI 為並列觀點，沒有先後順序；箭頭表示本圖的閱讀方向。

items.title: 使用者目標
items.body: 例如：完成銀行帳戶開立

items.title: UI：看見與操作
items.body: 表單、按鈕、資料提示、結果畫面

items.title: HCI：理解與判斷
items.body: 理解指示、選擇動作、解讀系統回饋

items.title: 系統處理與回饋
items.body: 檢查資料、儲存、通知、處理錯誤

items.title: UX：從開始到後續服務的整體結果
items.body: 是否完成開戶？過程是否順利？後續是否能使用帳戶？

paragraphs: 這個架構讓我們理解一件事：
軟體功能正確、介面容易使用，以及使用者真正完成任務，是三種不同層次的成功。
例如 AI 系統正確判斷申請資料齊全，並不代表使用者知道資料已經通過檢查；使用者知道資料齊全，也不代表申請程序已經完成。

sections.heading: 六、Usability（易用性）又是什麼？
paragraphs: 這是另一個容易與 UX 混淆的名詞。
Usability 通常翻成「易用性」或「可用性」，重點是特定使用者在特定情境下，能否有效、有效率且滿意地完成目標。
根據 ISO 9241-11:2018，可以從三個面向理解。
例如設計一台自助售票機，單純測量「買票要多久」還不夠。
如果操作速度很快，但部分使用者容易買錯車票，就不能說設計成功。
如果所有人都能買對車票，但第一次使用需要花十五分鐘，也可能有改善空間。
此外，還要考慮 Accessibility（無障礙使用）：例如是否能只透過鍵盤操作、是否支援輔助科技、文字是否容易閱讀。這些需求不應只被當作介面美化的附屬項目。

sections.heading: 七、實際案例：重新設計一個收件系統
paragraphs: 回到正式教材的情境。
假設我們正在設計政府機關的申請案件收件系統，承辦人必須確認申請資料，再匯出檢查報告。
原本的系統如下：

blocks.caption: 圖 4｜原本的設計與候選修改
blocks.description: 兩個示意介面並列比較；按鈕是示意文字。候選修改仍須透過真人任務測試驗證。

items.title: 原本的設計
items.body:
成功！

操作完成

確定

不清楚是什麼成功，也不知道是否已正式送件。

items.title: 候選修改
items.body:
欄位檢查完成

3 個必要欄位已齊全。

尚未正式受理。

匯出檢查報告

清楚說明已完成的事項及下一步，但仍須測試。

paragraphs: 這兩個都是示意介面，不代表真實使用者測試結果。

blocks.heading: 先從 HCI 找原因
paragraphs: 使用者看到「成功」時，腦中想到的是什麼？
我們可以請使用者直接回答：「你覺得現在這筆申請案處於什麼狀態？」
如果他認為已經送件，就表示系統表達的狀態和使用者理解的狀態不同。

blocks.heading: 接著透過 UI 提出修改
paragraphs: 不只是放大字體，而是明確區分「欄位齊全」、「檢查完成」、「正式送件」和「正式受理」等不同狀態，並提供下一步指引。
但要注意：如果後端系統根本沒有區分這些狀態，只改提示文字仍不足以解決問題。

blocks.heading: 最後從 UX 檢查完整工作
paragraphs: 就算承辦人順利匯出了報告，如果下一個承辦人拿到報告後，仍然需要重新查詢和填寫所有資料，整體工作仍然不順暢。
因此不能只測試「按鈕能不能按」，還要測試整段工作能否完成。

sections.heading: 八、如何證明我們真的改善了 UX？
paragraphs: 這一節是從設計走向工程驗證的關鍵。
我們不能因為 AI 說「已優化 UX」，就認為 UX 真的改善。
可以採取以下流程：

1. 定義使用者與任務：例如第一次使用系統的承辦人，需要找出缺少的資料並完成補正。
2. 觀察既有問題：記錄找不到欄位、看不懂提示、誤認為已經送件等具體情況。
3. 提出修改假設：在缺件欄位旁提供具體說明，應有助於使用者找到並修正問題。
4. 設計可比較的測試：讓具代表性的使用者在相近情境下操作既有版本與候選版本。
5. 評估結果：比較任務完成率、錯誤、完成時間及使用者解釋狀態的正確程度。
這裡有個重要區分：程式的單元測試能確認檢查邏輯是否符合規格，但不能直接證明真人看得懂訊息。
NIST 對 Usability Testing（易用性測試）的描述，也是讓具代表性的使用者執行具代表性的任務，再蒐集成功率、時間、錯誤及主觀感受等證據。

sections.heading: 九、AI 協作軟體工程：怎麼把這堂課真正用起來？
paragraphs: 未來請 AI Agent、ChatGPT 或其他 Coding Agent 設計介面時，應該避免只說：
> 幫我設計一個現代化、簡潔、漂亮的介面，UX 要很好。
因為這種描述沒有定義真正要解決的工作問題。
比較好的需求包含五個元素：

blocks.heading: 1. 誰使用
paragraphs: 第一次使用的承辦人

blocks.heading: 2. 要做什麼
paragraphs: 在案件資料中找出缺漏並完成修正

blocks.heading: 3. 遇到什麼困難
paragraphs: 只看到「資料錯誤」，不知道哪個欄位有問題

blocks.heading: 4. 要如何改善
paragraphs: 在對應欄位顯示具體錯誤、原因與修正方法

blocks.heading: 5. 如何證明有效
paragraphs: 讓使用者處理一個缺件案例，觀察能否自行理解並完成補正
如果要交給 AI 實作，可以使用這樣的指令：

blocks.heading: AI 設計需求範例
paragraphs: 以下指令先要求可檢查的設計稿，再列出真人測試假設。
這就是本課要建立的工程觀念：AI 不只是幫我們產生介面，也必須依照可觀察的使用問題進行設計，並讓結果能夠接受驗證。
blocks.code:
請設計一個供第一次使用的承辦人檢查與補正案件資料的網頁介面。

使用者任務：找出缺少的必要欄位並完成補正。
現有問題：系統只顯示「資料錯誤」，使用者不知道哪裡有問題。

設計假設：在欄位旁顯示具體錯誤原因與修正建議，可協助使用者自行完成補正。

要求：
- 區分欄位檢查完成、已送件、已受理等系統狀態。
- 提供清楚的下一步。
- 考慮鍵盤操作及錯誤復原。

請先產出文字線框稿、介面狀態與互動流程，不要直接開始寫程式。

最後列出需要透過真人任務測試驗證的假設，不得宣稱已改善 UX。

sections.heading: 與下一課的銜接
paragraphs: 這會銜接 M04-02 的 Task Analysis（任務分析）：在畫出介面前，先把使用者的工作步驟、角色、資訊需求與例外情境整理清楚。

sections.heading: 十、理解檢核
paragraphs: 請先自行作答，再展開參考解析核對理由。三題保留原有選項，另有一題實作練習。
本頁提供參考解析；可將自己的答案與理由另存，供討論或後續檢查。
本課最值得帶走的原則是：先理解人的工作與行為，再設計介面；最後用使用者完成任務的證據，判斷設計是否真正有效。

exercise.environment: problem.md、文字編輯器與合成收件情境；不需要改程式或接觸真人。
steps: 用同一缺件任務各寫一個 HCI、UI 與 UX 問題，保留操作前後的情境。
選一項困難，提出介面修改假設，說明要用什麼證據判斷。
將假設放入 wireframe-notes.md，和同儕核對是否把美觀或程式通過誤當成整體任務改善；單人可依檢核題自查。
exercise.expected: 一份包含三種分析觀點、具體修改假設及待驗方法的 wireframe-notes.md。
exercise.check: 能解釋三種觀點如何重疊；每個問題都有可觀察情境，沒有虛構研究結果。
exercise.cleanup: 保留合成標記與未知，移除真人姓名、案件內容與沒有用途的個人描述。

openChecks.prompt:
某銀行 APP 的轉帳按鈕很清楚，但使用者不明白「預約轉帳」和「立即轉帳」的差別。應優先從哪個角度研究原因？
UI
HCI
UX
answer: 優先從 HCI 研究使用者如何理解「預約轉帳」與「立即轉帳」。按鈕清楚只支持 UI 的可見性；可請使用者用自己的話解釋兩種轉帳的執行時點，再檢查文字、回饋與流程。

openChecks.prompt:
一個購物網站非常漂亮、操作快速，但消費者退貨時必須反覆致電客服，問題主要需要從哪個角度改善？
UI
HCI
UX
answer: 主要從 UX 檢查退貨的整段服務，包括聯絡、交接與退款。畫面漂亮及購物操作快速，仍不足以證明售後服務順暢。

openChecks.prompt:
AI 把錯誤訊息改得很清楚，程式測試也全部通過。是否就能證明 UX 已經改善？
可以，因為程式正確
不行，仍需要使用者任務證據
可以，因為文字更清楚
answer: 不行，仍需要使用者任務證據。讓具代表性的使用者處理缺件案例，觀察理解、錯誤、完成率及時間；單元測試只支持所測檢查邏輯。

openChecks.prompt: 實作題：請選醫療、銀行、物流或其他任一行業，提出一個 UI 修改假設，並說明如何驗證改善是否有效。
answer: 例如物流地址補正：在缺漏欄位旁顯示具體原因與修正方式，假設能協助使用者自行完成補正。以相近任務比較原版與候選版，記錄完成率、錯誤、時間、求助及狀態理解；測試前保留為假設。

en.summary: Use hospital check-in, six industries and an intake system to understand HCI, UI, UX, usability and verifiable AI design requirements.
objectives: Distinguish the scope of HCI, UI and UX through a work situation.
Identify differences among appearance, usability and overall task outcomes.
Propose an observable design hypothesis for an interface difficulty.

readingGuide.goal: Distinguish the scope of HCI, UI and UX through a work situation.
readingGuide.startingPoint: problem.md, a text editor and a synthetic intake scenario; no code changes or actual participants are needed.
readingGuide.route: Read the situation and principles, compare examples, then expand wireframe-notes.md and use the checks to review your understanding.
readingGuide.output: wireframe-notes.md with three analytical perspectives, a concrete design hypothesis and a planned verification method.

sections.heading: Help users understand the system and complete their work
paragraphs: The central idea of this lesson is that designing a system should help people understand it, operate it correctly and complete what they actually want to do.
This lesson uses everyday life, healthcare, banking, logistics, government services and AI software development as examples.

sections.heading: 1. Start with an everyday example
paragraphs: Imagine visiting a hospital and using its self-service check-in kiosk.
You insert your National Health Insurance card, confirm your appointment information, complete check-in and go to the consultation room to wait.
This apparently simple activity involves three different design questions.

blocks.caption: Figure 1 | Three design questions at hospital check-in
blocks.description: UI, HCI and UX are parallel perspectives; the user wants to receive medical care smoothly.

items.title: UI — User Interface
items.body:
How should buttons, typography, colors, prompts and card-insertion instructions appear on the kiosk?

For example: is “Confirm check-in” too small? Can older people read it?

items.title: HCI — Human–Computer Interaction
items.body:
How do people understand the instructions, decide what to do next and operate the kiosk?

For example: “Completed” makes a patient think check-in is done, but the system has only read the insurance card. Why does this misunderstanding happen?

items.title: UX — User Experience
items.body:
How is the whole experience of arrival, check-in, waiting, consultation, medication collection and departure?

For example: kiosk operation takes only 20 seconds, but the patient still gets lost because no consultation-room directions are given.

paragraphs: The important point in this example is:
An attractive, straightforward kiosk UI can still be part of a poor overall UX.
The user's actual task is to receive medical care smoothly, rather than merely operate the kiosk successfully.
This follows Nielsen Norman Group's view of UX: the experience covers the user's interactions with the product, service and organization as a whole. Appearance alone cannot establish its quality.

sections.heading: 2. What distinguishes the three concepts?
paragraphs: Compare their questions and methods to see what each perspective contributes.

blocks.caption: Table 1 | Compare HCI, UI and UX
rows: How do people understand and operate technology?
How does the interface present information and respond?
Does the whole experience meet their needs?
Completing the task and obtaining the service

paragraphs: HCI, UI and UX are not three completely separate work phases, nor does one necessarily contain the others.

HCI is an interdisciplinary research and design field; UI is the interface through which people interact with a system; UX concerns the quality of the overall experience. Their concerns overlap considerably.

blocks.caption: Figure 2 | Where HCI, UI, UX and interaction design meet
blocks.description: A conceptual illustration after Figma. Overlap indicates interacting concerns, not a strict academic classification of sets or three successive phases.

items.title: HCI | Human–computer interaction
items.body: Human cognition, behavior and interaction capabilities

items.title: UI | User interface
items.body: Screens, controls and responses

items.title: UX | User experience
items.body: Needs, outcomes and feelings across the service

items.title: IxD | Interaction design
items.body: Design interaction behavior and feedback where the three perspectives meet

paragraphs: Figma's conceptual illustration shows overlapping HCI, UI and UX concerns, with interaction design (IxD) at their intersection. It is a way to understand relationships, rather than a strict academic classification of sets.
UI is not limited to screens. A voice assistant's spoken prompts, a vehicle's physical control panel and an ATM's keys can all be user interfaces.

sections.heading: 3. HCI: why do users misunderstand a system?
paragraphs: HCI provides an important foundation: an engineer's knowledge of how the software works does not establish what users understand.
For example, a banking system displays “Review completed.”
The engineer may mean, “The system has finished checking whether all information is present.”
A bank employee may interpret it as, “This loan has been approved.”
The same message produces two different interpretations.
This involves an important HCI concept: the mental model.

blocks.heading: 1. Mental model: the user's internal map of system operation
paragraphs: When using an unfamiliar washing machine for the first time, you may expect pressing “Start” to begin washing immediately, based on previous experience.
This machine may first require you to select the water level, program and temperature.
The user's expectation and the system's actual behavior differ.
Good interaction design should align behavior with reasonable expectations, or provide enough information to help users form an accurate understanding.

blocks.heading: 2. Feedback: the system must respond after an action
paragraphs: Suppose you press “Pay” on a shopping website.
Nothing changes on screen.
You cannot tell whether payment succeeded, so you press again, potentially creating a duplicate order.
This is a feedback problem.
The system should make its current state clear: for example, “Processing payment,” “Payment successful; order number …” or “Payment failed; no charge was made.”

blocks.heading: 3. Error prevention: help avoid errors before displaying them
paragraphs: For example, a pharmacy system lets a pharmacist add medication to a collection list.
If a prescription has an unusual dosage, the system should provide more than a vague “Error code 203” at the end.
A better approach may identify the issue, help check the original prescription and require appropriate confirmation under professional procedures.
These designs concern how people understand information, make decisions and reduce operating errors.
These three concepts align with Nielsen's usability heuristics, including visibility of system status, familiar language and error prevention.

sections.heading: 4. Practice with six industries
paragraphs: The following hypothetical scenarios help you locate problems through different perspectives.

blocks.caption: Table 2 | Perspectives across six industries
rows: Patient thinks selecting a date completes booking
Patient cannot find check-in after arriving
Submit button is hard to notice
Customer confuses completeness checks with loan approval
Customer must re-enter information at a branch
Delivery status text is too small
Package goes to the wrong location and complaints are difficult
Chapter navigation is hard to find
Student does not know whether a quiz is complete
Student finishes the course but cannot apply it
Alarm message is hard to notice
Production cannot resume smoothly after the fault is cleared
User does not know whether AI is listening
Speech is recognized correctly but no appointment is completed

paragraphs: The table does not imply that each problem belongs to only one category.
For example, “Out for delivery” may simultaneously involve UI information presentation, HCI interpretation and a UX gap in delivery expectations.
The three perspectives complement one another rather than divide problems into mutually exclusive classes.

sections.heading: 5. Understand the relationship through user action
paragraphs: Read this simplified interaction structure from the user's goal to the overall outcome.

blocks.caption: Figure 3 | From a user goal to the overall outcome
blocks.description: A simplified teaching structure. Real use often cycles through action, feedback, interpretation and further action; HCI and UX extend beyond the scope shown here. UI and HCI are parallel perspectives, with no order between them; arrows indicate the reading direction of this illustration.

items.title: User goal
items.body: For example: open a bank account

items.title: UI: see and operate
items.body: Forms, buttons, information prompts and result screens

items.title: HCI: understand and decide
items.body: Interpret instructions, choose actions and interpret feedback

items.title: System processing and feedback
items.body: Check information, save, notify and handle errors

items.title: UX: overall outcome from start to follow-up service
items.body: Was the account opened? Was the process smooth? Can the account actually be used?

paragraphs: This structure highlights an important distinction:
Correct software behavior, an interface people can use, and users completing their actual task are three levels of success.

For example, AI correctly identifying complete application information does not establish that users know the check is complete. Knowing that information is complete also does not establish that the application procedure is finished.

sections.heading: 6. What is usability?
paragraphs: Usability is another term often confused with UX.
It concerns whether specified users, in a specified context, can achieve goals with effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction.
ISO 9241-11:2018 provides the framework for understanding these three dimensions.

blocks.caption: Table 3 | Usability and measurement
rows: Task completion rate and error rate
Completion time and number of actions

paragraphs: For a self-service ticket machine, measuring only how long buying a ticket takes is insufficient.
Fast operation with frequent purchases of the wrong ticket does not demonstrate successful design.
If everyone buys the correct ticket but a first attempt takes fifteen minutes, there may also be room for improvement.

Accessibility also matters: for example, keyboard-only operation, support for assistive technology and readable text. These requirements should be part of the design work rather than treated as decorative additions.

sections.heading: 7. Case study: redesign an application intake system
paragraphs: Return to the official lesson's scenario.
Suppose we are designing a government application intake system. Case workers must check the application information and export a check report.
Compare the original system with a candidate change.

blocks.caption: Figure 4 | Original design and candidate change
blocks.description: Two illustrative interfaces for comparison; the buttons are illustrative text. The candidate still requires human task testing.

items.title: Original design
items.body:
Success!

Operation completed

OK

It is unclear what succeeded or whether the application was formally submitted.

items.title: Candidate change
items.body:
Field check completed

3 required fields are complete.

Not officially accepted yet.

Export check report

It explains what has completed and the next action, but still needs testing.

paragraphs: Both interfaces are illustrations, not results from actual user testing.

blocks.heading: Start with HCI to investigate the cause
paragraphs: What does the user think when seeing “Success”?
Ask directly: “What state do you think this application is in now?”
If the answer is that it has been submitted, the state communicated by the system differs from the user's interpretation.

blocks.heading: Use UI design to propose a change
paragraphs: In addition to readable typography, distinguish “Fields complete,” “Check completed,” “Formally submitted” and “Officially accepted,” and explain the next action.
If the backend does not distinguish these states, changing message text alone will not resolve the problem.

blocks.heading: Use UX to examine the whole task
paragraphs: Even after a case worker exports the report, the workflow remains awkward if the next worker must look up and enter all information again.
Test whether the whole task can be completed as well as whether a button can be pressed.

sections.heading: 8. How can we demonstrate an improvement in UX?
paragraphs: This section connects design with engineering verification.
AI saying “UX optimized” does not establish an actual improvement.
Use the following process:

1. Define the user and task: for example, a case worker using the system for the first time must identify missing information and correct it.
2. Observe existing problems: record specific cases of fields being hard to find, prompts being misunderstood or applications being mistaken for submitted ones.
3. Propose a change hypothesis: specific guidance beside incomplete fields should help users find and correct problems.
4. Design comparable tests: representative users operate the existing and candidate versions under similar conditions.
5. Evaluate results: compare completion rates, errors, time and how accurately users explain the state.
Unit tests can establish whether checking logic meets its specification; they cannot directly establish whether people understand a message.
NIST describes usability testing as representative users performing representative tasks, with evidence such as completion rates, time, errors and subjective responses.

sections.heading: 9. Apply this lesson in AI-assisted software engineering
paragraphs: When asking an AI agent, ChatGPT or another coding agent to design an interface, avoid relying only on:
> Design a modern, simple, attractive interface with excellent UX.
This description leaves the actual work problem undefined.
A more useful requirement includes five elements:

blocks.heading: 1. Who uses it
paragraphs: A case worker using the system for the first time.

blocks.heading: 2. What they need to do
paragraphs: Find and correct missing information in an application.

blocks.heading: 3. What difficulty they face
paragraphs: They see only “Invalid information” and do not know which field has a problem.

blocks.heading: 4. What change to propose
paragraphs: Show the specific error, cause and correction method beside the relevant field.

blocks.heading: 5. How to demonstrate usefulness
paragraphs: Give users a missing-information case and observe whether they can understand it and complete the correction independently.
Use the following instruction when handing the work to AI.

blocks.heading: Example AI design request
paragraphs: This request first asks for reviewable design artifacts, followed by hypotheses requiring user testing.

The copyable request above is preserved in its original Chinese. In English: design a page for first-time case workers to check and correct application information. The task is to identify and fill missing required fields; the current problem is a generic “Invalid information” message that does not identify the affected field. The hypothesis is that specific causes and correction guidance beside each field help users complete corrections independently. Distinguish check completion, submission and acceptance; provide a clear next action; consider keyboard operation and recovery. Produce text wireframes, interface states and interaction flows before coding. Finally, list hypotheses requiring human task testing and do not claim an established UX improvement. This is the engineering principle of the lesson: AI should design against observable user problems and produce results that can be evaluated.
blocks.code:
請設計一個供第一次使用的承辦人檢查與補正案件資料的網頁介面。

使用者任務：找出缺少的必要欄位並完成補正。
現有問題：系統只顯示「資料錯誤」，使用者不知道哪裡有問題。

設計假設：在欄位旁顯示具體錯誤原因與修正建議，可協助使用者自行完成補正。

要求：
- 區分欄位檢查完成、已送件、已受理等系統狀態。
- 提供清楚的下一步。
- 考慮鍵盤操作及錯誤復原。

請先產出文字線框稿、介面狀態與互動流程，不要直接開始寫程式。

最後列出需要透過真人任務測試驗證的假設，不得宣稱已改善 UX。

sections.heading: Connection to the next lesson
paragraphs: M04-02, Task Analysis, builds on this: before drawing an interface, identify the user's work steps, roles, information needs and exceptional situations.

sections.heading: 10. Check your understanding
paragraphs: Try answering before opening the reference explanations. The three questions retain their original choices, followed by a practical exercise.
This page provides reference explanations. Save your own answers and reasoning separately for discussion or later review.
Take this principle forward: understand people's work and behavior, design the interface, then use evidence of users completing tasks to judge whether the design helps.

exercise.environment: problem.md, a text editor and a synthetic intake scenario; no code changes or actual participants are needed.
steps: Write one HCI, UI and UX question for the same missing-information task, retaining its surrounding context.
Choose one difficulty and propose an interface-change hypothesis with evidence to judge it.
Record the hypothesis in wireframe-notes.md. With a peer, check whether appearance or passing code was mistaken for overall task improvement; independent learners can use the checks.
exercise.expected: wireframe-notes.md with three analytical perspectives, a concrete design hypothesis and a planned verification method.
exercise.check: Explain how the perspectives overlap. Every question has an observable situation without invented research results.
exercise.cleanup: Keep synthetic labels and unknowns. Remove actual names, case content and unnecessary personal descriptions.

openChecks.prompt:
A banking app has a clear transfer button, but users do not understand the difference between “Scheduled transfer” and “Immediate transfer.” Which perspective should you prioritize when investigating the cause?
UI
HCI
UX
answer: Prioritize HCI: investigate how users interpret “Scheduled transfer” and “Immediate transfer.” A visible button supports UI visibility only. Ask users to explain when each transfer executes, then examine wording, feedback and workflow.

openChecks.prompt:
A shopping website is attractive and fast, but returning a purchase requires repeated calls to customer service. Which perspective mainly helps address the problem?
UI
HCI
UX
answer: Use UX to examine the full returns service, including contact, handoffs and refunds. An attractive screen and fast purchasing flow do not establish smooth after-sales service.

openChecks.prompt:
AI makes an error message clearer and all program tests pass. Does this establish that UX has improved?
Yes, because the program is correct
No, evidence from users performing tasks is still needed
Yes, because the wording is clearer
answer: No: evidence from users performing tasks is still needed. Representative users should handle missing-information cases while you observe understanding, errors, completion and time. Unit tests support only the checking logic exercised.

openChecks.prompt: Practical exercise: choose healthcare, banking, logistics or another industry. Propose a UI change hypothesis and explain how to test whether it helps.
answer: For example, hypothesize that specific reasons and correction guidance beside incomplete delivery-address fields help users correct them independently. Compare existing and candidate versions on similar tasks, recording completion, errors, time, help and state understanding. Keep it a hypothesis until tested.
